doc.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Manhattan School of Music clarinet course and the move to Juilliard
summary: Studying clarinet because no school taught saxophone, leaving Manhattan School of Music and transferring to Juilliard, and the joy of being a music student in New York.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: was Ray Chase, and even his watch didn’t keep time, you know what I mean? [MN laughs] He had a big, he had a ratchet and gongs, and a big Chinese cymbal, and he had a couple of pops, and he’d want to play “The World is Waiting for a Sunrise” very, what he thought was fast. And it was awful. But it was a summer gig and it paid for my … that following year I entered Manhattan School of Music as a clarinet major for a summer course.
They didn’t teach sax, did they at the time?
They didn’t teach saxophone at the time, did they?

No, no no. Saxophone was not, no, it was the yeomen of the military bands, that’s what the saxophone was, according to one of the orchestration books. Yes, the saxophone, a yeomen of the military bands, I never forgot that. Classic.

And then I transferred to Julliard. I didn’t care for the, I didn’t care for the uh for Manhattan, I mean for something me and the clarinet teacher didn’t hit it off, but I do remember being in the middle of Manhattan going to Manhattan School of Music which was in the, in the, in East Harlem, with that new kind of Latin section, Puerto Rican section. And I went to classes and I loved education, you know, loved just learning about music, man it was all part of the same thing, I didn’t want to learn Bebop I just wanted to be a musician, you know. And I remember getting a shaved ice on the street, you know, and they shaved the ice and put some raspberry syrup or something on it. And I’m standing in the middle of Lenox Avenue or something and I just yell “Yay! I’m in New York and I’m having a shaved ice and I’m learning music,” I mean and I never forget that, that joyous feeling of music making. And to this day I think that if it’s not a joy, if it’s not fun I want no part of it. And I really…that’s almost 70 years later, 65 at least and I still have, I’m still a very joyful player. I love I love what I do, you know? I love it. I… It gets more precious the older I get.
